summary: APA Monitor Apr 2024: experts on both sides agree hypnosis enables special focused attention; neuroimaging finds 'little consensus' on brain regions/networks; Terhune (KCL) attributes this to the varied phenomena hypnosis is used to study. Three networks (CEN, SN, DMN) + lingual gyrus emerging.
content: APA Monitor on Psychology, April 2024 ('Uncovering the new science of clinical hypnosis'): APA Division 30 defines hypnosis as 'a state of consciousness involving focused attention and reduced peripheral awareness characterized by an enhanced capacity for response to suggestion' (Elkins et al. 2015). 'The definition of hypnosis has been the subject of debate for the better part of a century.' Both sides agree hypnosis 'allows for a special kind of focused attention that opens people up to suggestion.' Devin Terhune (KCL): 'Neuroimaging studies have found little consensus in pinpointing brain regions and networks involved in hypnotic states and suggestions... If you look across the literature, some studies use hypnosis to induce visual hallucinations, others to modulate pain or memory. Given these very different phenomena, it's not that surprising that we don't find a single brain region or network.' Raz et al. review found three networks (CEN, SN, DMN) + lingual gyrus. DMN activity 'seems to go down in hypnotic states' (Lifshitz, McGill). Faerman & Spiegel: higher hypnotizability correlates with lower perseveration (more cognitive flexibility).
